candidate.title: E-Signature Document Phishing Scam
candidate.summary: Scammers send an unexpected email that looks like it's from a law firm, DocuSign, or another e-signature service, urging you to "review and sign" an attached document right away, when the real goal is to steal your data or install malware.
safetyTips: Never click links or open attachments in an unsolicited e-signature request; instead, go directly to the sender's official website in a new browser tab to verify
Call the supposed sender using a phone number you look up independently, not one provided in the email, to confirm the document is real
Hover over (don't click) any link to check where it actually leads before trusting a 'review document' or 'sign now' button
Watch for odd phrasing, generic greetings, or small inconsistencies in formatting, which can indicate a forged document even when AI writing makes grammar look clean
Report suspicious e-signature emails to the FTC and to the e-signature provider or firm being impersonated
candidate.howItWorks: The scam arrives as an email impersonating a law firm or a well-known e-signature brand, with urgent subject lines about a document awaiting your electronic signature. In one widespread November 2025 version, the sender posed as "Rigsby Law Group" of Lexington, Kentucky; the email read "Important – Your attention is needed for a document awaiting review and your electronic signature today"
redFlags: Receiving a signature request for a document you never expected, from a firm or person you don't recognize or haven't dealt with recently
The sender's email domain is inactive, misspelled, or doesn't match the real organization's official domain when checked independently
A link that looks like it goes to an e-signature or document service but actually points somewhere else, such as a generic Google Doc or unrelated site when you hover over it
Urgent, vague language insisting you review and sign 'today' without naming a specific deal, case, or transaction
A request to log in, enter personal/financial details, scan a QR code, or download a file to 'view' the document
realExamples: ConsumerAffairs confirmed a November 2025 phishing email impersonating 'Rigsby Law Group' of Lexington, Kentucky, asking recipients to electronically sign an attached document; the firm confirmed the message was fraudulent and the link actually led to a Google document rather than a legitimate e-signature company.
The Identity Theft Resource Center reported its own employees received phishing emails claiming to have an invoice awaiting signature through services mimicking DocuSign and HelloSign.

A consumer alert described a version impersonating 'DocuSign Electronic Service' that asks recipients to log in to sign a document or download a fraudulent invoice, delivering spyware or ransomware or harvesting personal and financial information.

triage.reasoning: This is a specific instance of a phishing email impersonating a law firm/e-signature request to steal data or install malware, which fits within the broader existing 'Phishing Email Scam' category rather than being a structurally distinct pattern; the law firm/e-signature framing is a thematic variant, not a new mechanism.
